# Review without a queue: what Chen and Stratton (2026) mean for an autonomous system

*An Ultrastable white paper. Ultrastable is the foundation for any autonomous system.*

## Executive summary

Many people believe that AI writes more code, so a team must review more code, and review becomes the bottleneck. This paper argues otherwise: review is a bottleneck only when a person is the gate. Replace the queue with checks that can fail, live verification and automatic revert, and measure quality instead of waiting.

We map each of their findings to the mechanisms Ultrastable uses instead of a human review queue, and test each mapping against this system's own records.

It is written for people who build or run AI systems and want them to keep working without someone watching. It names 7 concrete problems, the mechanism that answers each one, and how to put that mechanism in place.

## 1. The problem

AI coding tools raise code output substantially but final software output only a little, with no detectable employment effect. Code review becomes the bottleneck: code waits longer for a reviewer, spends longer in review and draws more requested changes. [1]

This matters now because the usual answer, more AI code means a bigger human review queue, sends teams after the wrong fix. A better model or another reviewer does not close a loop that nothing checks.

The problems in detail:

1. More code is not more shipped work. After AI agent adoption, pull requests opened rise 35.7% while resolved issues (work deployed to production) rise only 13.7%; increases above 30.7% are ruled out. [1]
2. Review becomes the bottleneck. After AI agent adoption, the time from a pull request's submission to its merge rises 56.1%: waiting for a reviewer rises 59.9% and time in active review 58.5%. [1]
3. System-made changes wait longer than session-made ones. The study's model predicts that when review capacity is fixed, the waiting time grows with the volume of submitted code. A system that writes its own changes must not let its own pull requests queue behind human-driven ones. [1]
4. Lower code quality raises review effort and risk. After agent adoption the share of changes receiving a review comment rises 13.1% and comments per change rise 38.6%; interviewees report outages caused by AI-generated commits. [1]
5. Unverified deploys reach production. Code must be reviewed and tested before it can be deployed; the study treats review as the quality gate that AI-written code strains. [1]
6. AI review tools leave humans in the loop. 79.1% of firms adopted AI code review tools, but the overwhelming majority of reviews and comments are still written by people, so the bottleneck persists. [1]
7. One approver is a single point of failure. Reviewers mostly review code they already know (82.8% versus 17.2% at random); an interviewee describes one senior engineer as the only approver, reviewing once a week. [1]

## 2. The approach

The approach follows Ashby's ultrastable system [2]: a first loop acts on the world, and a second loop changes the first loop's settings whenever a variable that matters leaves its limits, and keeps changing them until it is back inside.

Ultrastable is that design as working code [3]. For each problem above it uses a specific mechanism:

1. More code is not more shipped work: the system's own score counts verified live deploys, never commits or lines (CRITICALITY-1, `foundation/criticality.py`); the public progress page lists merged and shipped work only; record-keeping merges are excluded (PROGRESS-1, `site/progress.js`)
2. Review becomes the bottleneck: a server-side lane merges a green pull request without waiting for a person (AUTO-SHIP-CLEAN-1, `seed/worker/src/sweeper.js`); the tick Worker owns merge, deploy and live verification after a pull request opens (HANDOFF-1, `seed/worker/src/handoff.js`); a green pull request left open fails a check (DRAIN-ZERO-1, `foundation/lanewatch.py`)
3. System-made changes wait longer than session-made ones: the lane takes every open pull request until none is left (DRAIN-ALL-1, `.github/workflows/lane.yml`); work the system originates on itself is ranked first when the regime is driven (SELF-REFERENCE-1, `foundation/criticality.py`)
4. Lower code quality raises review effort and risk: a model change that elides or stubs code is refused before it becomes a pull request (ELISION-1, `foundation/executor.py`); a red main is repaired by reverting the smallest change that broke it (REDMAIN-1, `foundation/redmain.py`); every failure mode has a live detector and a queue item (FAILURE-RESOLVE-1, `foundation/failure_audit.py`)
5. Unverified deploys reach production: every deploy runs a verify line against production and rolls back on failure (HANDOFF-1, `seed/worker/src/handoff.js`); freshness of each live source is served and probed (FRONT-BACKED-1, `site/live.js`)
6. AI review tools leave humans in the loop: no step waits on a person reading, reviewing or approving (CLOSED-LOOP-1, `foundation/closedloop.py`); human touches are counted every tick and lower the score (CRITICALITY-1, `foundation/criticality.py`)
7. One approver is a single point of failure: every single point of failure, approvals included, is registered and remediated (GUIDING-DIRECTIVE section 12, `doctrine/registers.json`); every merge and deploy path has a second route needing no person's credential (NO-SINGLE-ROUTE, `foundation/failover.py`)

## 3. Putting it into practice

To apply this to your own system, one step per problem:

1. More code is not more shipped work. Put in place: the system's own score counts verified live deploys, never commits or lines. Check it with one number, verified live deploys per merged pull request in the same window, and set a limit for it (>= 0.5 is the limit we use).
2. Review becomes the bottleneck. Put in place: a server-side lane merges a green pull request without waiting for a person. Check it with one number, median hours from a pull request opening to its merge, and set a limit for it (<= 1.0 is the limit we use).
3. System-made changes wait longer than session-made ones. Put in place: the lane takes every open pull request until none is left. Check it with one number, median hours to merge for pull requests the system's own workflows or App opened, and set a limit for it (<= 2.0 is the limit we use).
4. Lower code quality raises review effort and risk. Put in place: a model change that elides or stubs code is refused before it becomes a pull request. Check it with one number, commits on main whose subject starts with Revert, per merged pull request in the window, and set a limit for it (<= 0.05 is the limit we use).
5. Unverified deploys reach production. Put in place: every deploy runs a verify line against production and rolls back on failure. Check it with one number, share of uploaded deploys proven live against their commit, and set a limit for it (>= 0.95 is the limit we use).
6. AI review tools leave humans in the loop. Put in place: no step waits on a person reading, reviewing or approving. Check it with one number, share of merged pull requests opened by the system itself, and set a limit for it (>= 0.5 is the limit we use).
7. One approver is a single point of failure. Put in place: every single point of failure, approvals included, is registered and remediated. Check it with one number, verified deploys the system originated and executed itself (latest criticality tick), and set a limit for it (>= 1 is the limit we use).

In our own system, 5 of 7 of these checks pass today. Verified live deploys per merged pull request in the same window reads 1.967 (n = 360; source: ops/deploys.jsonl and the pull request snapshot). Median hours from a pull request opening to its merge reads 0.14 (n = 360; source: GitHub REST pulls?state=closed, last 500 closed pull requests, fetched 2026-11-26T21:44:41Z). Median hours to merge for pull requests the system's own workflows or App opened reads 0.13 (n = 47; source: GitHub REST pulls?state=closed, last 500 closed pull requests, fetched 2026-11-26T21:44:41Z). Where a check fails, a work item carries the fix, and it closes only when the same check passes.

## 4. Trade-offs and limits

- Scale. One organization: 500 closed pull requests (360 merged) over 7.85 days, against a study of 655 firms over more than five years. Our numbers describe this system; they are not a causal estimate and are not compared with the study's effect sizes as if they were.
- Who wrote the changes. 87% of merged pull requests in the window were opened by code agent sessions run under the owner's account, not by the system's own loops. The latest criticality tick puts the system in the driven regime with 0 self-originated deploys, so most of the work measured here was started from outside.
- Review by construction. Ultrastable has no human review step, so a short open-to-merge time is partly a consequence of the design. The real test of the design is quality: the revert and deploy-verification findings, which can fail.
- Revert share counts commits whose subject starts with Revert; a fix that undoes a change without that word is not counted, so the figure is a lower bound.
- Source. Job market paper (working paper, not peer reviewed), version 2026-11-19 (first version 2026-01-07); its findings may change in later versions.
